name: Sorbic acid
text:
Sorbic acid is an organic acid first isolated from the berries of the rowan tree (Sorbus aucuparia), hence its name. Virtually all sorbic acid used today is made synthetically. It prevents the growth of moulds and yeasts and works best below about pH 6.5.

It is found in foods such as cheese, bread and other baked goods, fruit juices, dried meats, smoked fish, margarine and sauces.

Sorbic acid and its salts have very low toxicity in mammals.

name: Sodium sorbate
text:
Sodium sorbate is the sodium salt of sorbic acid, an unstable white solid. Like other sorbates, it acts against moulds and yeasts; sorbate salts are generally preferred to the acid itself because they dissolve better in water.

In 1965 the FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA considered it too unstable for satisfactory use in food. In its 2015 re-evaluation of sorbates, EFSA noted positive results for sodium sorbate in genotoxicity tests, which look for damage to genetic material.

name: Potassium sorbate
text:
Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt of sorbic acid, made by neutralising sorbic acid with potassium hydroxide. It is a white salt that is very soluble in water and is used to stop moulds and yeasts from growing.

Typical uses include cheese, wine, yogurt, dried meats, cider, dried fruit, soft drinks and baked goods. In sweetened wines it is added before bottling to prevent renewed fermentation.

Sorbic acid and its salts have very low toxicity in mammals.

name: Calcium sorbate
text:
Calcium sorbate is the calcium salt of sorbic acid. Like other sorbates, it was used as a preservative against moulds and yeasts.

In 2018 the EU removed it from its list of food additives, with effect from August that year. In 2015 the European Food Safety Authority had found that genotoxicity data on calcium sorbate were lacking and could not confirm its safety, and no business operator offered to provide the missing studies.

name: Heptylparaben
text:
Heptylparaben (heptyl p-hydroxybenzoate) is the heptyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid. It belongs to the parabens, a family of preservatives active against a broad range of microorganisms, and is used as a food preservative.

It is also produced naturally by some microorganisms, including bacteria of the genus Microbulbifer.

name: Benzoic acid
text:
Benzoic acid is the simplest aromatic carboxylic acid. It occurs naturally in many plants; most berries contain appreciable amounts, and cranberries and bilberries are especially rich in it. Food-grade benzoic acid is made synthetically.

It inhibits moulds, yeasts and some bacteria, and its effect depends on acidity, so it is used in acidic foods and drinks such as fruit juices, soft drinks and pickles.

Concern has been raised that benzoic acid and its salts can react with vitamin C in some soft drinks to form small amounts of benzene, a carcinogen.

name: Sodium benzoate
text:
Sodium benzoate is the sodium salt of benzoic acid, made by neutralising benzoic acid with sodium hydroxide. In acidic foods it turns into benzoic acid, which inhibits moulds, yeasts and some bacteria; the salt is used because the acid itself dissolves poorly in water.

It is common in carbonated drinks, fruit juices, jams, pickles, salad dressings and condiments.

Together with vitamin C, benzoates can form benzene in drinks, and heat, light and long storage increase this. In 2006 US tests, a few drinks exceeded the drinking-water limit for benzene; most were later reformulated.

name: Potassium benzoate
text:
Potassium benzoate is the potassium salt of benzoic acid, made by neutralising benzoic acid with potassium hydroxide. It inhibits moulds, yeasts and some bacteria and works best in acidic products below about pH 4.5, where it is present as benzoic acid.

It is used in fruit juices, carbonated and other soft drinks, and pickles. Like sodium benzoate, it can form benzene in drinks that also contain vitamin C.

It has low acute toxicity when swallowed.

name: Calcium benzoate
text: Calcium benzoate is the calcium salt of benzoic acid. Like the other benzoates, it is used as a preservative against moulds, yeasts and some bacteria in acidic foods and drinks, where it acts in the form of benzoic acid.

name: Ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate
text:
Ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate, better known as ethylparaben, is the ethyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid and a member of the parabens. It is used as an antifungal preservative in food; parabens in general are also widely used in cosmetics and medicines.

In 2004 the European Food Safety Authority set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 10 mg per kg of body weight for methyl and ethyl parabens and their sodium salts.

name: Sodium ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate
text:
Sodium ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate is the sodium salt of ethylparaben and has the same uses: it serves as an antifungal food preservative.

In 2004 the European Food Safety Authority set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 10 mg per kg of body weight for methyl and ethyl parabens and their sodium salts.

name: Propylparaben
text:
Propylparaben is the propyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid, a paraben that occurs naturally in some plants and insects and is also made synthetically. It is a common preservative in cosmetics and medicines, and in food it has been used, for example, in packaged pastries and tortillas.

The EU withdrew propylparaben and its sodium salt (E217) as food additives in 2006. In 2004 the European Food Safety Authority had found that, unlike methyl and ethyl parabens, it affected sex hormones and male reproductive organs in juvenile rats, and it could not set an acceptable daily intake.

name: Sodium propyl p-hydroxybenzoate
text:
Sodium propyl p-hydroxybenzoate is the sodium salt of propylparaben and was used in the same way, as an antifungal food preservative.

The EU withdrew it together with propylparaben (E216) as food additives in 2006, after the European Food Safety Authority found in 2004 that propylparaben affected sex hormones and male reproductive organs in juvenile rats and could not set an acceptable daily intake.

name: Methyl p-hydroxybenzoate
text:
Methyl p-hydroxybenzoate, better known as methylparaben, is the methyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid. Parabens are inexpensive, colourless, odourless and stable, and are among the most common preservatives in cosmetics and foods; methylparaben acts mainly against fungi.

In animal studies it is practically non-toxic when swallowed; the body converts it to p-hydroxybenzoic acid and excretes it in urine without accumulation. In 2004 the European Food Safety Authority set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 10 mg per kg of body weight for methyl and ethyl parabens and their sodium salts.

name: Sodium methyl p-hydroxybenzoate
text:
Sodium methyl p-hydroxybenzoate is the sodium salt of methylparaben. It is used as a preservative in food, medicines and cosmetics, where it helps extend shelf life by acting against microorganisms.

In 2004 the European Food Safety Authority set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 10 mg per kg of body weight for methyl and ethyl parabens and their sodium salts.

name: Sulphur dioxide
text:
Sulphur dioxide is a colourless gas with a pungent smell, the smell of burnt matches. Most of it is made by burning sulphur.

In food it is used for its antimicrobial and antioxidant effects, for example in dried apricots, figs and other dried fruit, where it also keeps the colour. It has been used in winemaking since Roman times and protects wine from bacterial spoilage and from oxidation and browning.

Some people with asthma are sensitive to sulphites, and reactions can be serious. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Sodium sulphite
text:
Sodium sulphite is a white, water-soluble salt made industrially by treating sulphur dioxide with a solution of sodium carbonate. It is used as an antioxidant and preservative: as a reducing agent it keeps dried fruit from discolouring, and it is also used in preserving meat.

Sulphites can cause breathing difficulties within minutes in sensitive people, especially some with asthma, though severe reactions are rare. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Sodium hydrogen sulphite
text:
Sodium hydrogen sulphite, also called sodium bisulphite, is not a single compound but a mixture of salts that dissolve in water to give sodium and bisulphite ions. It forms white or yellowish-white crystals that smell of sulphur dioxide.

In food it prevents discolouration, bleaches food starches and delays spoilage.

JECFA has set an acceptable daily intake for sulphites of 0 to 0.7 mg of sulphur dioxide equivalent per kg of body weight. Some sensitive people, notably some with asthma, react to sulphites. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Sodium metabisulphite
text:
Sodium metabisulphite, also called sodium pyrosulphite, is an inorganic salt that forms sodium bisulphite when dissolved in water. It is used as a preservative, antioxidant and disinfectant.

In winemaking it acts as an antimicrobial and antioxidant. It is also used to keep chipped potatoes from discolouring in storage and to preserve fruit during shipping.

Some sulphite-sensitive people can have allergic reactions to it, sometimes severe. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Potassium metabisulphite
text:
Potassium metabisulphite, also called potassium pyrosulphite, is a white crystalline powder with a pungent smell. In wine or grape must it forms sulphur dioxide, which acts as a disinfectant and a strong antioxidant, protecting the colour and flavour of the wine. Its solutions are also used to sanitise winemaking equipment.

It is also used in brewing and as a preservative in lemon juice and some pickles.

It may cause allergic reactions in some sensitive people. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Potassium sulphite
text:
Potassium sulphite is a salt of potassium and sulphite, a white solid that is highly soluble in water. It is used for preserving food and beverages.

Like other sulphites, it can cause reactions in sensitive people, particularly some with asthma.

name: Calcium sulphite
text:
Calcium sulphite is the calcium salt of sulphite and forms white solids. As a food additive it is a preservative; like other sulphites, it acts as an antioxidant by scavenging oxygen.

Sulphites are commonly used in preserving wine, cider, fruit juice and canned fruit and vegetables.

Some people are hypersensitive to sulphites. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Calcium hydrogen sulphite
text:
Calcium hydrogen sulphite, or calcium bisulphite, is an acid salt made by treating lime with an excess of sulphur dioxide and water. It is used as a food preservative, for example for brining cherries, and in the sulphite process for making paper from wood.

Sulphites can trigger asthma attacks in susceptible people and can cause hives and swelling in otherwise healthy individuals. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Potassium hydrogen sulphite
text:
Potassium hydrogen sulphite, or potassium bisulphite, is not a single compound but a mixture of salts that gives potassium and bisulphite ions in water. It is a white solid that smells of sulphur dioxide and is made by passing sulphur dioxide through a potassium carbonate solution.

It is used as a sterilising agent in the production of alcoholic beverages.

Sulphites can cause reactions in sensitive people, particularly some with asthma. In the EU, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg per kg or per litre must be declared on the label.

name: Biphenyl
text:
Biphenyl, also called diphenyl, is an aromatic hydrocarbon that forms colourless crystals. It prevents the growth of moulds and other fungi and was used as a preservative, particularly to protect citrus fruit during transport.

Its main industrial use is as a heat-transfer fluid, mixed with diphenyl ether.

In the EU it was listed as a preservative for the surface treatment of citrus fruit until a 2003 directive took it out of the food additive rules, because such treatment falls under the legislation on plant protection products (pesticides).

name: Orthophenyl phenol
text:
Orthophenyl phenol, or 2-phenylphenol, is a white solid used mainly as an agricultural fungicide. It is applied to citrus fruit after harvest, as part of the wax coating.

It is also a general surface disinfectant used in households, hospitals, farms and food processing plants. When used as a fungicide in food packaging, it may migrate into the food.

In the EU it was listed as a preservative for the surface treatment of citrus fruit until a 2003 directive took it out of the food additive rules, because such treatment falls under the legislation on plant protection products (pesticides).

name: Sodium orthophenyl phenol
text:
Sodium orthophenyl phenol is the sodium salt of 2-phenylphenol. It is used as a disinfectant and as a preservative for treating the surface of citrus fruit.

In the EU it was listed as a food preservative for that purpose until a 2003 directive took it out of the food additive rules, because such treatment falls under the legislation on plant protection products (pesticides).

name: Thiabendazole
text:
Thiabendazole is a fungicide and antiparasitic agent. It is used mainly against mould, blight and other fungal diseases of fruit and vegetables; for example, it is applied to bananas and added to the waxes that coat citrus peel.

As a medicine for people and animals, it treats roundworm, hookworm and other worm infections.

In the EU it was listed as a food additive for the surface treatment of citrus fruit and bananas until 1998, when the entry was deleted because thiabendazole is covered by the rules on pesticide residues.

name: Nisin
text:
Nisin is an antibacterial peptide produced by the bacterium Lactococcus lactis. For food use it is obtained by culturing the bacterium, not by chemical synthesis. It acts against many Gram-positive bacteria, including Listeria and Clostridium botulinum, and is particularly effective against spores.

It is used in processed cheese, meats and beverages to extend shelf life, typically at about 1 to 25 parts per million.

name: Natamycin
text:
Natamycin, also called pimaricin, is an antifungal substance produced by fermentation of Streptomyces bacteria; it was first isolated in 1955 from Streptomyces natalensis. It acts against moulds and yeasts by binding to ergosterol in their cell membranes.

In food it is used on the surface of certain cheeses and dry sausages to prevent mould. It is also a medicine for fungal eye infections.

In 2009 EFSA judged the proposed use levels for surface treatment of these cheeses and sausages to be safe.

name: Formic acid
text:
Formic acid is the simplest carboxylic acid. It occurs naturally in most ants, in the stinging hairs of nettles and in small amounts in many fruits and vegetables. Industrially it is produced from carbon monoxide.

Its main use is as a preservative and antibacterial agent in livestock feed, including silage. It is also used in leather tanning and textile dyeing. It has low toxicity, but the concentrated acid is corrosive to the skin.

name: Sodium formate
text:
Sodium formate is the sodium salt of formic acid, a white powder that readily absorbs moisture. It is usually made by neutralising formic acid with sodium hydroxide. Together with formic acid, it occurs naturally in the stinging hairs of nettles.

It inhibits some species of bacteria. Besides its use as a food additive, it is used in fabric dyeing and printing, as a buffering agent and as a de-icer on airport runways.

name: Calcium formate
text:
Calcium formate is the calcium salt of formic acid. Industrially it is formed as a co-product in the manufacture of trimethylolpropane, or made from calcium hydroxide and carbon monoxide.

Under the number E238 it is used as a preservative in animal feed: it acidifies the feed, which slows microbial growth and extends shelf life. It is also used in leather tanning, as an additive to cement and grout, and as a de-icer.

name: Hexamethylene tetramine
text:
Hexamethylene tetramine, also called hexamine or methenamine, is a synthetic compound made from formaldehyde and ammonia. Under acidic conditions it breaks down to formaldehyde, which gives it its antimicrobial effect. It is also used as a urinary antiseptic medicine and in solid fuel tablets.

As a food additive it is used in Provolone cheese. In 2014 EFSA concluded that this use, at a residual level of up to 25 mg/kg expressed as formaldehyde, is not of safety concern.

name: Formaldehyde
text:
Formaldehyde is a pungent, colourless gas, mainly used to make industrial resins. Its water solutions are used as disinfectants and to preserve tissue samples. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies it as a known human carcinogen, associated with cancers of the nose and nasopharynx.

Formaldehyde occurs naturally in many foods at low levels. It has also been added to foods such as noodles, tofu and salted fish to extend their shelf life, which caused food scares in Indonesia and Vietnam in the 2000s.

name: Dimethyl dicarbonate
text:
Dimethyl dicarbonate (DMDC) is a colourless liquid used as a beverage preservative. It is highly active against the yeasts, bacteria and moulds that spoil drinks.

It is added before bottling and then breaks down into small amounts of methanol and carbon dioxide, both natural constituents of fruit and vegetable juices. It is used in wine, cider and non-alcoholic drinks such as juice drinks, iced teas and flavoured waters. In wine it can replace potassium sorbate against spoilage yeasts such as Brettanomyces.

name: Ethyl lauroyl arginate
text:
Ethyl lauroyl arginate (LAE) is a synthetic surfactant derived from lauric acid, the amino acid arginine and ethanol. It acts against a broad range of bacteria, moulds and yeasts by damaging the cell membranes of microbes.

Studies in rats showed that it is rapidly broken down to lauroyl arginine and arginine, which is further metabolised to ornithine and urea. In the EU it is used in cooked meat products. It is also a preservative in cosmetics and an active ingredient in some mouthwashes.

name: Glycolipids
text:
Glycolipids are compounds in which a sugar is bound to a fatty part. The food additive E246 is a purified mixture of long-chain glycolipids obtained by fermentation of the edible fungus Dacryopinax spathularia. It is used as a preservative in drinks such as flavoured drinks and alcohol-free beer, where it acts against yeasts, moulds and some bacteria.

In its 2021 evaluation, EFSA found that these glycolipids are very poorly absorbed when swallowed and that animal studies showed no adverse effects. It set an acceptable daily intake of 10 mg/kg body weight and found no safety concern at the proposed uses.

name: Potassium nitrite
text:
Potassium nitrite is an inorganic salt, a white or slightly yellow crystalline powder. It is used in curing meat in the same way as sodium nitrite: nitrite slows the growth of Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that causes botulism, and gives cured meats their pink colour and characteristic flavour.

Nitrites can form nitrosamines during curing, when cured meat is cooked and in the acidic stomach. IARC classifies ingested nitrite under conditions that lead to such formation in the body as probably carcinogenic to humans.

name: Sodium nitrite
text:
Sodium nitrite is an inorganic salt, a white to slightly yellowish crystalline powder, best known as an additive in processed meats. It speeds up curing, inhibits Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that causes botulism, gives ham, bacon and hot dogs their pink colour and helps delay rancidity. In meat processing it is always mixed with ordinary salt as curing salt.

Nitrites can form nitrosamines during curing, when cured meat is cooked and in the acidic stomach. IARC classifies ingested nitrite under conditions that lead to such formation in the body as probably carcinogenic to humans.

name: Sodium nitrate
text:
Sodium nitrate, also known as Chile saltpetre, occurs naturally as the mineral nitratine, with the largest deposits in Chile and Peru. It is also made industrially from nitric acid and sodium carbonate.

In food it is used as a preservative and colour fixative in cured meats and poultry. Nitrosamines formed in cured meats containing nitrate and nitrite have been linked to stomach and oesophageal cancer. EFSA estimated in 2017 that nitrate from food additives makes up less than 5% of total dietary nitrate exposure.

name: Potassium nitrate
text:
Potassium nitrate, known as saltpetre, occurs in nature as the mineral nitre and is also produced industrially, for example by neutralising nitric acid with potassium hydroxide. It has been used to salt meat since antiquity or the Middle Ages and gives processed meats a red colour.

It has largely been replaced by sodium nitrite, which works faster and more consistently, but it is still used in some salami, dry-cured ham and corned beef. EFSA estimated in 2017 that nitrate from food additives makes up less than 5% of total dietary nitrate exposure.

name: Acetic acid
text:
Acetic acid is the active component of vinegar. It is produced both by bacterial fermentation and synthetically: most acetic acid is made by carbonylation of methanol, while the fermentation route remains important for vinegar.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and condiment. Vinegar, its dilute solution, is used directly as a condiment and for pickling vegetables and other foods.

name: Potassium acetate
text:
Potassium acetate is the potassium salt of acetic acid, a solid that readily absorbs moisture. It can be made by treating a potassium base such as potassium hydroxide with acetic acid.

In processed foods it is used as a preservative and acidity regulator. Outside food it is used as a de-icer for aircraft and runways, in some fire extinguishers for burning cooking oil, and in medicine as a diuretic.

name: Sodium acetates
text:
The sodium acetates are sodium salts of acetic acid: sodium acetate and sodium diacetate. Sodium acetate is made by treating acetic acid with sodium hydroxide; sodium diacetate forms when acetic acid is half-neutralised.

Sodium acetate is used to control pH and extend shelf life. Sodium diacetate is used as a preservative and antimicrobial agent and to give a salt and vinegar flavour, for example in salt and vinegar crisps.

name: Calcium acetate
text:
Calcium acetate is the calcium salt of acetic acid. It can be prepared by treating calcium carbonate, such as limestone, or hydrated lime with vinegar.

As a food additive it acts as a stabiliser, buffer and sequestrant, mainly in sweets. It can also replace calcium sulfate for coagulating soy milk when making tofu. In medicine it is used to bind dietary phosphate in people with kidney disease.

name: Ammonium acetate
text:
Ammonium acetate is the ammonium salt of acetic acid, a white solid that readily absorbs moisture. It is made by neutralising acetic acid with ammonia or ammonium carbonate.

As a food additive it is used as an acidity regulator. It is also used in laboratories as a buffer, for example in mass spectrometry and liquid chromatography, and as a diuretic.

name: Dehydroacetic acid
text:
Dehydroacetic acid is a synthetic organic compound, a colourless to white crystalline powder that is almost insoluble in water. It is made industrially by dimerisation of diketene.

It acts as a fungicide and bactericide. As a food preservative it has been used on squash and strawberries. Its sodium salt, sodium dehydroacetate (E266), is often used instead because it dissolves better in water.

name: Sodium dehydroacetate
text:
Sodium dehydroacetate is the sodium salt of dehydroacetic acid and dissolves in water more readily than the acid. It is a preservative effective against a broad range of bacteria even at low concentrations.

Its food uses include pickled vegetables, fermented soy products, seasonings, bread and pastries, and it can give food an acetic odour. It is also a preservative in cosmetics and personal care products such as shower gels.

name: Buffered vinegar
text:
Buffered vinegar is vinegar partly neutralised with sodium or potassium hydroxides and carbonates. It is made as a liquid or a dried product, and its main constituents are acetic acid and its salts (acetates). The vinegar comes from agricultural sources. It is used as a preservative and acidity regulator, for example in cheese, fresh pasta, bread and meat preparations.

In the body it breaks down to acetate, a normal part of the diet and of the human body. In 2022 EFSA found no safety concern at the proposed maximum and typical use levels.

name: Lactic acid
text:
Lactic acid is an organic acid found in fermented foods such as yogurt, kefir, sourdough bread, pickled vegetables, fermented sausages and some beers. It is also produced in the human body during normal metabolism and exercise.

The additive is mostly made by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates such as glucose or sucrose, and partly by chemical synthesis. It is used as a preservative, curing agent and flavouring in processed foods, and to decontaminate meat during processing.

name: Propionic acid
text:
Propionic acid is a naturally occurring carboxylic acid, an oily liquid with a pungent smell. Propionibacteria produce it, and their activity contributes to the odour of Emmental cheese. Propionate is also among the most common short-chain fatty acids produced by gut bacteria from dietary fibre.

Industrially it is mainly made from ethylene. It inhibits moulds and some bacteria at 0.1 to 1% by weight, and about half of world production is used to preserve animal feed and food.

name: Sodium propionate
text:
Sodium propionate is the sodium salt of propionic acid, a white crystalline solid made by reacting propionic acid with sodium carbonate or sodium hydroxide.

It is used as a food preservative, mainly as a mould inhibitor in bakery products. Like calcium propionate, it is effective against both moulds and rope, a bacterial spoilage of bread caused by Bacillus mesentericus.

name: Calcium propionate
text:
Calcium propionate is the calcium salt of propionic acid. It is used as a preservative in bread and other baked goods, processed meat, whey and dairy products, and works only in relatively acidic foods with a pH of 5.5 or below.

In bakery products it acts as a mould inhibitor, typically added at 0.1 to 0.4%, and also protects against rope, a bacterial spoilage of bread. In agriculture it is used to prevent milk fever in cows.

name: Potassium propionate
text: Potassium propionate is the potassium salt of propionic acid. It can be prepared by treating potassium carbonate with propionic acid, and it is used as a food preservative.

name: Boric acid
text:
Boric acid is a weak acid of boron, usually seen as colourless crystals or a white powder. It occurs in nature as the mineral sassolite and can be made from borax. It is used as an antiseptic, insecticide and flame retardant.

Its food use is as a preservative for sturgeon eggs (caviar). In its 2013 re-evaluation, EFSA noted that boron harms the male reproductive system at high doses in animal studies, set a group acceptable daily intake for boron and judged regular exceedance unlikely.

name: Sodium tetraborate (borax)
text:
Sodium tetraborate, commonly called borax, is a salt of boric acid. It occurs naturally in evaporite deposits left by seasonal lakes and can also be made from other boron compounds. It has many household and industrial uses, including as an insecticide and in glass and enamels.

In food it is used as a preservative for sturgeon eggs (caviar), and it gives food a firm, rubbery texture. In its 2013 re-evaluation, EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for boron, based on effects in animal studies, and judged regular exceedance unlikely.

name: Carbon dioxide
text:
Carbon dioxide is a colourless gas present in the atmosphere and odourless at normal concentrations. It is a by-product of fermentation, for example in brewing, and of industrial processes such as hydrogen production. Its solid form is dry ice.

In food it is used as a propellant and acidity regulator. It makes soft drinks and soda water fizzy, and beer and sparkling wine are often carbonated with carbon dioxide recovered from fermentation. Dissolved carbon dioxide is converted to carbonic acid, giving carbonated drinks a sour taste.

name: Malic acid
text:
Malic acid is a dicarboxylic acid made by all living organisms. It is the main acid in many fruits, including apricots, cherries, grapes, plums and pears, and contributes to the sourness of unripe apples, from which it was first isolated.

Only the L-form occurs naturally; industrially produced malic acid is a mixture of the L- and D-forms. It is sometimes used with or instead of citric acid in sour sweets, and such sweets may carry a warning that eating too many can irritate the mouth.

name: Fumaric acid
text:
Fumaric acid is an organic acid that occurs widely in nature, for example in fumitory, bolete mushrooms, lichens and Iceland moss. It is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, and human skin produces it when exposed to sunlight. Industrially it is made from maleic acid.

It has been used as a food acidulant since 1946. It serves as an acidity regulator in drinks and baking powders, generally as a substitute for tartaric acid, and in wheat tortillas as a preservative and as the acid in leavening.
